history.ask: What the patient means by dizzy
options: Unsteady on the feet without spinning
Turning over in bed or looking up sets it off
One-sided hearing loss or fullness during attacks
Viral illness in the past 2 weeks
Double vision, slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, or limb clumsiness
New headache or neck pain with the vertigo
Known migraine, attacks with light/sound sensitivity
Heavy menstrual bleeding or black stools

red_flags: Vertigo with double vision, slurred speech, dysphagia, limb weakness, or clumsiness
Inability to stand or walk unaided (severe truncal ataxia)
Acute vertigo with new severe headache or neck pain
Vertigo with acute deafness (beyond typical Meniere pattern)
Vertigo in a patient > 60 with vascular risk factors or atrial fibrillation — assume posterior circulation stroke until examined
Dizziness with syncope, exertional presyncope, or palpitations and an abnormal pulse
exam: Measure lying then standing BP at 1 and 3 minutes — a drop ≥ 20/10 mmHg rules in orthostatic hypotension
Palpate the pulse for a full minute — irregularly irregular rhythm (AF) raises both arrhythmic presyncope and cardioembolic stroke
Perform the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre — brief torsional up-beating nystagmus after a latency confirms posterior-canal BPPV
Perform the head impulse test in continuous vertigo — a corrective saccade indicates peripheral (vestibular neuritis); a NORMAL head impulse with continuous vertigo is a stroke signal
Observe nystagmus direction in different gaze positions — direction-changing or vertical nystagmus indicates a central cause
Test of skew: alternate cover — vertical corrective movement indicates a central cause (completes HINTS)
Test cerebellar function: finger–nose, rapid alternating movements, heel–shin
Assess gait and Romberg — mild sway is peripheral; inability to stand unaided is central until proven otherwise
Screen cranial nerves: eye movements, facial symmetry, speech, swallow
Perform otoscopy — vesicles (zoster), middle-ear disease as vertigo sources
Whisper test or tuning fork for one-sided hearing loss (Meniere, labyrinthitis)
Inspect conjunctivae for pallor (anaemia as light-headedness driver)

investigations.why: Rules in arrhythmia (AF, AV block, long QT) when the story is light-headed presyncope with palpitations; AF also raises cardioembolic posterior-circulation stroke risk
Low haemoglobin rules in anaemia as the cause of non-vertiginous light-headedness — pairs with the bleeding-screen question and pallor on exam
Hypoglycaemia mimics presyncopal dizziness in treated diabetics — a low value during symptoms settles it
Dehydration (raised urea) supports orthostatic hypotension after vomiting/diarrhoea; sodium and potassium abnormalities cause both light-headedness and arrhythmia

investigations.test: Postural BP measurement recorded as a test
investigations.why: The formal lying/standing readings are themselves the diagnostic test for orthostatic hypotension — documenting the drop rules it in and spares imaging
Documented low-frequency sensorineural loss on the affected side rules in Meniere disease against BPPV and vestibular neuritis, which spare hearing

investigations.test: Brain MRI with diffusion (or CT if MRI unavailable)
investigations.why: Second-line — mandatory when HINTS is central, ataxia is severe, or focal signs exist: rules posterior-circulation stroke in or out; note early CT is often normal in posterior fossa stroke, so a normal CT does not close the question
For recurrent unexplained presyncopal episodes with normal resting ECG — captures paroxysmal arrhythmia as the cause

supports: Seconds-long spinning triggered by turning in bed or looking up
No hearing loss or neurological company
Positive Dix-Hallpike with latency and fatigable torsional nystagmus
Continuous severe vertigo for days after a viral illness
Abnormal head impulse test with unidirectional horizontal nystagmus
Can still stand with support; no dysarthria or diplopia
Hearing loss present only in labyrinthitis
Spontaneous vertigo attacks lasting 20 minutes to hours
One-sided fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness
Low-frequency sensorineural loss on audiometry
Acute vertigo with diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, or limb ataxia
Normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, or skew deviation
Cannot stand unaided
Age > 60 with vascular risk factors or AF
Recurrent vertigo minutes to hours in a known migraineur
Light/sound sensitivity or headache with some attacks
Normal hearing and normal exam between attacks
Light-headedness on standing, not spinning
New/changed BP medication or volume loss (vomiting, diarrhoea)
Documented postural drop ≥ 20/10 mmHg
Light-headed episodes with palpitations or on exertion
Irregular pulse or abnormal resting ECG
Arrhythmia captured on Holter during a symptomatic episode
Constant light-headedness with fatigue and exertional dyspnoea
Conjunctival pallor; menorrhagia or black stools on history
Low haemoglobin on CBC
